title: Man Deploys AI Songs and 10,000 Bots to Scam $8 Million in Music Royalties, Prosecutors Reveal
body:
A North Carolina resident has been sentenced to 18 months behind bars after a federal jury found that he orchestrated a sophisticated scheme that used artificial‑intelligence‑generated songs and a network of up to 10,000 automated accounts to siphon more than $8 million in music‑streaming royalties. Prosecutors said the defendant, identified only as “the defendant,” exploited the algorithms of popular streaming platforms, inflating play counts on fabricated tracks and diverting the resulting payments to accounts he controlled.

The fraud, which unfolded over several years, hinged on the rapid advances in generative AI that can compose melodies, arrange instrumentation and even produce vocal performances with minimal human input. By feeding these AI‑crafted compositions into a cloud‑based distribution service, the defendant was able to list thousands of “songs” on major platforms such as Spotify, Apple Music and Amazon Music. Each track was then streamed repeatedly by a legion of bot accounts that mimicked the behavior of genuine listeners—clicking, pausing, and replaying songs to satisfy the platforms’ detection algorithms. The cumulative effect was a steady flow of royalty checks that were deposited into bank accounts linked to the defendant’s operation.

Legal experts note that the case underscores a growing vulnerability in the digital music ecosystem, where royalty calculations are largely automated and rely on reported stream counts. “The technology that makes it easy to generate a song in seconds also makes it easy to game the system,” said Laura Mitchell, a professor of entertainment law at the University of Southern California. “What we’re seeing is a convergence of two trends: the democratization of music creation through AI and the insufficient safeguards against synthetic traffic on streaming services.” The prosecution argued that the defendant’s use of up to 10,000 bots at any given time demonstrated a level of coordination more akin to a cyber‑crime operation than a typical piracy case.

The Department of Justice’s investigation was sparked after a whistleblower from a digital rights management firm flagged irregular streaming patterns associated with a cluster of newly released tracks that bore strikingly similar waveform signatures. Subsequent forensic analysis traced the IP addresses of the streaming activity to a series of proxy servers located in multiple countries, all routing back to a single hosting provider used by the defendant. In addition to the prison term, the court ordered restitution of $8.2 million to the affected streaming platforms and imposed a lifetime ban on the defendant’s participation in any music‑related business.

Industry reaction has been swift. The Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) issued a statement calling the verdict “a decisive message that manipulation of streaming data will not be tolerated.” Streaming services, meanwhile, have pledged to invest in more robust detection tools, including machine‑learning models designed to differentiate human listening behavior from bot‑generated traffic. Some analysts predict that the cost of implementing such safeguards could be passed on to artists and labels in the form of higher fees, a development that may reignite debates over the fairness of the current royalty distribution model.

Looking ahead, the case may set a legal precedent for how courts treat AI‑driven fraud in the creative sector. As generative technologies become increasingly accessible, regulators are expected to tighten oversight of both content creation and distribution pipelines. Lawmakers are already drafting legislation that would require streaming platforms to verify the authenticity of stream sources and to disclose the use of AI‑generated works. If enacted, these measures could curb the profitability of similar schemes and restore confidence in the digital music marketplace, ensuring that royalties flow to genuine creators rather than to automated fraudsters.
